title: Liquid Penetrant Testing for Mining | Dye Penetrant (US)
description: Dye penetrant inspection for US mines: manganese steel parts, stainless leach plant piping, aluminum, weld repairs, cylinder rods. On-site PT. Get a quote.
h1: Liquid Penetrant Testing for Mining and Mineral Processing Equipment in the United States
html:
Liquid penetrant testing (PT), often called dye penetrant inspection, reveals cracks that reach the surface of any non-porous material, magnetic or not. In mining that makes it the method for austenitic manganese steel wear parts, stainless piping in hydrometallurgical plants, aluminum and bronze components, and weld repairs where magnetic particle work is impractical. Atlantis NDT sends technicians to US mines and plants for the agreed scope. To begin, request a PT inspection quote.

Why penetrant testing matters at a mine

Magnetic particle testing is the default for cracks in carbon steel, and most mining structure is carbon steel. But a surprising amount of mine equipment is not. Crusher liners, bucket teeth and wear plates are commonly austenitic manganese steel, which stays non-magnetic even after work hardening. Process plants that leach, extract and refine metals use stainless steels, duplex grades and nickel alloys because acid solutions destroy carbon steel. Conveyor drive components use aluminum and copper alloys. None of these can be examined by magnetic particle methods, and PT is the practical choice for finding surface cracks in them.

PT is also used when the geometry or the site is awkward for a yoke: tight fillets, threaded holes, the root of a gear tooth, a hydraulic fitting. If a part is magnetic and the crack could lie below the surface, the better tool is covered on the magnetic particle page or the page for ultrasonic testing in mining.

Parts and systems we examine with PT

  • Austenitic manganese steel. Jaw and cone crusher liners, mantles, concaves, bucket teeth, and hammers. Cracks start in work-hardened skin and on casting surface defects. PT on the surface after grinding shows both.
  • Stainless and duplex process piping. Pipework, tanks and agitators in leach, solvent extraction and electrowinning circuits. Chloride and acid service can cause stress corrosion cracking at welds and heat-affected zones.
  • Weld repairs on any alloy. After a crack is ground out and rewelded, PT on the repair confirms removal before the part goes back into service.
  • Hydraulic cylinder components. Rod ends, clevises, gland threads and welded cylinder bases on shovel and dozer hydraulics.
  • Aluminum and bronze parts. Truck body panels and bracket castings in aluminum, and bronze bushings and wear rings on heavy machinery.
  • Threaded and machined features. Studs, thread relief, bearing housing bores and gear tooth roots where fatigue cracks hide in corners.

Standards, regulators and acceptance

MSHA enforces safe equipment under 30 CFR Parts 56 and 57 for metal and nonmetal mines and Parts 75 and 77 for coal, without prescribing a PT procedure. The examination follows ASME Section V Article 6, the commonly specified penetrant method, with ASTM E165 as the practice and ASTM E1417 for the process controls and material qualification. Where a specification requires it, penetrant materials for stainless steel and nickel alloys must be checked for sulfur and halogen content. Weld acceptance usually refers to AWS D1.1 for structures or AWS D14.3 for equipment, or the manufacturer's repair criteria. The article on Section V Article 6 sets out the requirements in plain language.

Acceptance belongs to the owner, the maker or the engineer of record. Our report applies the stated criterion to each indication and the owner decides how to repair. Technicians work under the Atlantis written practice based on ASNT SNT-TC-1A: Level II technicians perform and interpret, and an ASNT Level III approves procedures and reviews reports.

How the process works on site

  1. Clean. Remove paint, oil, scale and grinding smear. On manganese steel and machined aluminum, smeared metal can close a crack, so we grind or etch lightly where the procedure allows.
  2. Apply penetrant. Visible solvent-removable red penetrant is typical in the field because no darkness is needed. Fluorescent penetrant is more sensitive but requires a dim shelter and an ultraviolet lamp.
  3. Dwell. The penetrant sits long enough to enter fine cracks. The time depends on the material and the defect type and is set in the procedure.
  4. Remove excess. Wipe with solvent-dampened cloth in the same direction, taking care not to flush penetrant out of cracks.
  5. Apply developer. A thin white coating draws penetrant out of cracks so it appears as a red line.
  6. Inspect and record. Read the indications in the specified light, mark and photograph them, then post-clean the part.

Temperature, weather and surface conditions

Penetrant systems are qualified for a stated range, commonly roughly 40 to 125 degrees Fahrenheit. A cold morning in northern Minnesota or Alaska can fall below that, and a hot Arizona truck frame in the sun can sit well above it. If the part is outside the range, we warm or cool the area, or qualify the procedure at the actual temperature as the code allows. Wind and dust spoil developer coatings and contaminate surfaces, so tents help. Remote sites often have no running water, so solvent cleaners and wipes are used rather than water-washable systems.

Weld repairs and rebuilds: where PT is used most

Mines weld constantly. Cracked truck components are gouged out and rewelded, worn buckets are rebuilt with hardfacing, and cast parts are repaired in the shop. Each repair has two inspection points where penetrant testing is valuable. The first is after the crack has been ground or gouged out and before any weld metal goes in: PT on the excavation shows whether the whole crack has been removed, which is the single most common reason repairs fail. The second is after welding and grinding, when the repair is examined again to the acceptance criteria. On carbon steel, MT can do both steps, but PT is often preferred in the excavation because arc strikes and carbon-gouge residue interfere with magnetic particle patterns. Hardfacing overlays crack by design to relieve stress; the procedure should state which check cracking is acceptable and which cracks that reach the base metal are not.

Planning a mine visit

As with every mining job, the operator controls access. Site-specific hazard training under 30 CFR Part 46 or Part 48 is arranged before technicians arrive, and we ask for the safety contact when you inquire. Penetrant testing generates solvent-wetted rags and aerosol cans, so we agree where waste goes and whether the mine restricts chemicals in certain areas such as electrical rooms and process tanks. For plants with acid solution, confined-space entry and process isolation come first. We schedule around the shutdown window and confirm dates with your planner rather than promising a fixed arrival.

What PT finds and what it cannot see

PT shows only defects open to the surface. A crack closed by smeared metal, filled with oxide or covered by paint will not draw penetrant. It cannot find subsurface flaws, and rough surfaces such as as-cast liners hold penetrant that causes background. We therefore recommend surface preparation and sometimes light grinding before testing. When a component may have flaws below the surface, we suggest UT instead. Atlantis does not perform radiography in the US, and other techniques beyond MT, PT and UT are not offered here.

Typical choice by mining material
MaterialExamplesMethod
Carbon and low alloy steelTruck frames, booms, pinsMT first, PT when MT is impractical
Manganese steelLiners, teeth, hammersPT for surface, UT for thickness
Stainless and duplexLeach plant pipe and tanksPT with controlled materials
Aluminum and bronzeBody brackets, bushingsPT

What the PT report contains

Each report gives the component and location, the procedure and revision, the penetrant and developer brand and batch numbers, the cleaner, the application method, the dwell time, the part and ambient temperatures, the lighting and the technician with qualification level. Indications are listed with position, length and shape, photographed, and judged against the named acceptance criteria. After testing the parts are post-cleaned, particularly stainless and nickel alloys, so residues do not remain on process surfaces. A Level III reviews and signs the report before release.

What to send for a quote

  • A list of parts or systems with the alloy, thickness and surface finish.
  • Photographs, drawings or weld maps showing the areas to be examined.
  • The specification or code that sets acceptance and any special material limits.
  • Where the work occurs, access needs, and who supplies water, power and lighting.
  • Site address and MSHA training requirements, along with permits and the shutdown window.

Training your own technicians in PT

PT is among the easiest methods for a maintenance team to learn, and quality problems usually come from cleaning and dwell mistakes, not from the chemistry. Atlantis offers PT Level 1 training and PT Level 2 training, and practice on the penetrant testing simulator. Since the employer certifies under SNT-TC-1A, your written practice governs; written practice development helps draft it. See the national penetrant testing page and the comparison of MT versus PT when picking a method for a new component.

faq.q: Why is penetrant testing used on crusher liners instead of magnetic particle testing?
faq.a: Austenitic manganese steel is not magnetic, so magnetic particle methods cannot work on it. Penetrant testing finds surface-breaking cracks regardless of magnetism, which makes it the practical choice for liners, mantles, teeth and hammers once the surface has been cleaned.

faq.q: Can PT be done on a hot haul truck component?
faq.a: Standard penetrants are qualified for a limited temperature range, so a part heated in the sun or by operation may need to cool, or the procedure must be qualified at that temperature. We measure surface temperature before starting and record it in the report.

faq.q: Is penetrant safe for stainless steel process piping?
faq.a: It can be, if the penetrant materials are controlled for low sulfur and halogen content and the part is cleaned afterward. We use qualified materials where the specification calls for it and post-clean thoroughly so no residue stays on product-contact surfaces.

faq.q: Can you test welds in a leach or electrowinning plant?
faq.a: Yes, for surface cracks and incomplete weld repairs on stainless, duplex and nickel alloy pipe and tanks. We work around process isolation, lock-out and confined-space rules set by the plant, and we post-clean afterward.

faq.q: What if the surface is rough or painted?
faq.a: Rough surfaces and coatings hide cracks and cause background. We normally ask for paint removal and local grinding at the test area, then record the condition. If grinding is not allowed on a part, we tell you what the examination can and cannot show.

faq.q: How accurate is dye penetrant testing at finding cracks?
faq.a: It is very sensitive to open surface cracks when the part is clean and the dwell is correct, but it only finds defects open to the surface. The report states the limits. For flaws below the surface the better method is UT.

faq.q: What do you need to quote PT at our mine?
faq.a: Send a parts list with materials and surface finish, photographs or drawings, the acceptance code, access and utilities arrangements, and the site address with training requirements. We reply within one business day to confirm scope and what we need.

faq.q: Who decides what to do with a rejected indication?
faq.a: The owner, the equipment maker or the engineer. We report each indication against the named criterion, and repairs or scrapping are your decision. We can re-examine the part after a repair using the same procedure.

faq.q: Can you do X-ray or gamma-ray inspection of mine welds?
faq.a: No. Industrial radiography in the United States is licensed under federal or Agreement State radiation rules, and Atlantis does not perform it. For radiographic work the owner hires a licensed firm, and we can review the radiographs as a Level III service.
